body_html:
Spain slang can surprise learners who studied Latin American Spanish. In Madrid or Barcelona, you will hear tío and tía for people who aren’t relatives, guay and mola for anything cool, and vale at the end of almost every sentence. Many of these words would sound strange in Mexico, and some Mexican words sound odd in Spain. Here are the words Spaniards use most, what they mean, how casual they are and which ones are rude.

Quick answer
  • Everyday and safe: vale, guay, mola, tío/tía, majo
  • Casual: flipar, currar, pasta, chaval, en plan
  • Rude or vulgar: hostia, joder, coño, very common but strong.
  • Spain uses vosotros, so slang often comes with it: ¿Qué hacéis, tíos?
{{toc}}

Spain slang for everyday conversations

WordMeaningExample
valeokayVale, nos vemos a las ocho. (Okay, see you at eight.)
guaycool¡Qué guay tu chaqueta! (What a cool jacket!)
molait’s cool, I like itMe mola este bar. (I really like this bar.)
tío / tíadude, guy / girlTío, ¿dónde estás? (Dude, where are you?)
majo / majanice, friendlyTu novia es muy maja. (Your girlfriend is really nice.)
fliparto be amazed¡Flipé con el concierto! (The concert blew my mind!)
currar / el curroto work / jobMañana curro todo el día. (I’m working all day tomorrow.)
la pastamoneyNo tengo pasta. (I have no money.)
el chavalkid, young guyEs un chaval muy listo. (He’s a very smart kid.)
cutreshabby, cheapEl hotel era un poco cutre. (The hotel was a bit shabby.)

Vale is the word you will hear most. It means “okay”, “sure” or “got it”, and Spaniards use it the way Americans use “okay”. In Mexico, people say va, sale or órale instead.

Going out: quedar, la caña and la marcha

WordMeaningExample
quedarto meet up¿Quedamos el sábado? (Shall we meet on Saturday?)
una cañaa small draft beer¿Nos tomamos unas cañas? (Shall we have a few beers?)
ir de tapasto go out for tapasVamos de tapas por La Latina. (Let’s go for tapas in La Latina.)
la marchanightlife, partyingMadrid tiene mucha marcha. (Madrid has great nightlife.)
el botellóndrinking outdoors in a groupHacían botellón en el parque. (They were drinking in the park.)
estar hecho polvoto be exhaustedEstoy hecho polvo. (I’m wiped out.)

For the different meanings of quedar, see {{link:quedar-vs-quedarse|quedar vs quedarse}}.

{{image:2}}

Conversation fillers: en plan, o sea, es que

Spaniards, especially younger people, fill their sentences with small words. En plan works a lot like “like” in American English: Estaba en plan… no sé qué decir (I was like… I don’t know what to say). O sea means “I mean”, and es que introduces an excuse or explanation: Es que no tengo tiempo (It’s just that I don’t have time).

I cover these in more detail in {{link:spanish-filler-words|Spanish filler words}}.

Words that are rude in Spain

Spain is famous for strong language in everyday speech. Words that would shock people in Mexico are common among friends in Spain, but they are still vulgar:

  • ¡Hostia! or ¡Hostias!: “Wow!” or “Damn!” Very common, but rude in formal settings.
  • ¡Joder!: “Damn!” or worse. Heard everywhere, still a swear word.
  • coño: vulgar, used as an exclamation.
  • gilipollas: “idiot”, offensive.

Also note a classic trap in the other direction: coger simply means “to take” or “to catch” in Spain (coger el autobús), but it is vulgar in Mexico and much of Latin America. See {{link:embarrassing-spanish-mistakes|embarrassing Spanish mistakes}}.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

A sample chat between friends

Marta: ¡Hola, tío! ¿Quedamos esta noche?
Hey, dude! Shall we meet up tonight?

Pablo: Vale, pero estoy hecho polvo. Hoy he currado diez horas.
Okay, but I’m exhausted. I worked ten hours today.

Marta: Venga, solo unas cañas. Hay un bar nuevo que mola mucho.
Come on, just a few beers. There’s a new bar that’s really cool.

Pablo: Bueno, vale. Pero invitas tú, que no tengo pasta.
Okay, fine. But you’re paying, I’ve got no money.

Venga (come on) is another word you will hear constantly in Spain, both to encourage and to end a conversation: ¡Venga, hasta luego!

Spain slang vs Mexican slang

SpanishEnglish
vale / va, saleokay (Spain / Mexico)
guay, mola / chido, padrecool (Spain / Mexico)
tío / güeydude (Spain / Mexico)
pasta / lanamoney (Spain / Mexico)
curro / chambajob (Spain / Mexico)
caña / chelabeer (Spain / Mexico)

Both sets are understood across most of the Spanish-speaking world thanks to TV and movies, but using the local version makes you sound much more natural. For Mexico, see {{link:mexican-slang|Mexican slang}}.

{{image:3}}

Common mistakes

  • Calling someone tío in a formal setting. It is friendly, not polite.
  • Using vosotros slang in Latin America. Latin Americans use ustedes for everyone.
  • Thinking hostia is harmless. It is everywhere, but it is still a swear word.
  • Confusing majo with mono. Majo means nice; mono means cute in Spain.

The RAE dictionary marks many of these words as colloquial and lists where they are used.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Spain slang is friendly, fast and full of vale. Learn the everyday words, recognize the rude ones, and remember that much of it is specific to Spain. For slang from other countries, see my complete guide to {{link:spanish-slang|Spanish slang}}.

faq.q: What is the most common slang word in Spain?
faq.a: Vale (okay) is the most frequent, followed by tío/tía, guay and mola.

faq.q: Why do Spaniards call people tío?
faq.a: It is friendly slang for “dude” or “guy”, used among friends, not only for actual uncles.

faq.q: Is Spain slang understood in Mexico?
faq.a: Mostly, thanks to TV and movies, but it sounds foreign. Locals use their own words.
Yes. It is extremely common in Spain, but it is a swear word and inappropriate in formal settings.
